newsitem.title: USA: Reno unveils steps to modify U.S. immigration law.
newsitem.headline: Reno unveils steps to modify U.S. immigration law.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno on Thursday unveiled three steps to fulfil President Bill Clinton's pledge to help Central American and other immigrants facing deportation under a tough, new U.S. law.

She told a Justice Department news conference the steps were aimed at making sure the law applied mainly to cases that arose after April 1, when it took effect, rather than those cases that had been pending at the time.

Reno said she will consider overturning an immigration ruling on the law, that legislation will be sent to Congress to end certain parts of the law and that administrative measures may be adopted if Congress fails to act.
At issue were provisions of the law that set tougher standards for immigrants seeking to avoid deportation and that established a quota of 4,000 exceptions a year.

Reno said the steps were designed to find "a fair and reasonable solution" for thousands of Central Americans and others whose cases were pending when Congress changed the standard for humanitarian relief from deportation.
Her announcement seeks to carry out Clinton's assurances made at a one-day summit in Costa Rica in May to Central American leaders that he will not allow mass deportations under the law.
Reno estimated that as many as 280,000 people may be eligible to avoid deportation. Justice Department aides said the vast majority of those affected were from El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua.

Under the proposed legislation to be sent to Congress next week, applicants for suspension of deportation whose cases were pending before April and who met the standards then in effect, would receive relief on a case-by-case basis.
"It is not an amnesty," Reno emphasised.

In a letter to House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, Reno said that if the legislation was not adopted, the administration will consider taking action on its own, including deferring enforced departures of certain Central American immigrants.

Reno also said she would review and consider overturning a Board of Immigration Appeal decision that prevented many aliens who were in immigration proceedings before April from having their requests for suspension of deporation considered.
